title: Job-Order Costing & Cost Codes to WIP GL (CMA P1-D · feeds FAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — one invoice, two ledgers

MBG structure: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 in account series 14xxxxx as work in progress. That total must be useful in two different ways. The general ledger must show controllable financial-statement categories, while the job-cost ledger must tell a project manager which job, phase, and activity consumed the money. Posting a framing invoice directly to a made-up GL account named after the cost code destroys that separation. The correct architecture is: detailed cost code for job tracking, mapped to a real WIP control account for the debit, with the vendor liability credited. MBG uses JCS as its job-cost GL; do not call it Ledgerline 100. MBG and Riverton also remain entity-segregated.

The salvaged mapping engine makes the rule explicit. Labor codes roll to 1401, materials to 1402, equipment to 1403, subcontractors to 1404, and other direct costs to 1405. Cost codes such as L004, M001, E001, S003, and O001 are dimensions, not GL accounts. A clean posting preserves both views without multiplying the chart of accounts.

Concept — job-order costing from first principles

Job-order costing accumulates costs for a distinct job, contract, or batch. It fits construction because each home or project has its own scope, estimate, change orders, and margin. A job-cost record normally captures the entity, job, cost code, cost type, amount, date, source document, and approver. The GL captures the financial account. The two records must reconcile: the sum of job detail mapped to a WIP control account must equal that control account's GL balance for the same entity and cutoff.

Three classifications matter. Direct costs can be traced economically to one job: jobsite lumber, crew time, a dedicated excavator rental, or a framing subcontract. Indirect production costs support multiple jobs and require a rational allocation, such as shared supervision or equipment depreciation. Period costs support the company rather than production and are expensed when incurred, such as general corporate administration. Classification determines whether a cost enters WIP, is allocated to jobs, or hits current expense.

The source document starts the control trail. A purchase order establishes authorization; receiving evidence establishes occurrence; the vendor invoice establishes the amount; job and cost-code approval establish classification. Payroll follows a parallel trail through approved time, PayStream ACH or MBG check, and job allocation. There is no cash labor. The posting engine should reject an invalid cost code and should never accept a cost code as the GL account.

The five-account rollup

Job-cost categoryIllustrative codeMapped WIP GL
LaborL004 Rough carpenter1401 WIP — Labor
MaterialsM001 Framing lumber1402 WIP — Materials
EquipmentE001 Excavator rental1403 WIP — Equipment
SubcontractorS003 Framing1404 WIP — Subcontractors
Other directO001 Permits and fees1405 WIP — Other direct costs

These account numbers and mappings are real app mapping rules. The sample transaction amounts below are illustrative because the source materials provide MBG's total WIP but not invoice-level amounts for these five codes.

Worked example — post, roll up, and reconcile

Assume an illustrative MBG framing package for Job H-101 contains $8,400 of framing lumber coded M001, $3,200 of rough-carpenter labor coded L004, and a $12,500 framing subcontract coded S003. Each line keeps Job H-101 and its cost code. The financial postings are:

AccountDebitCredit
1402 WIP — Materials$8,400—
1401 WIP — Labor$3,200—
1404 WIP — Subcontractors$12,500—
Cash/AP/payroll liabilities, as applicable—$24,100

The job-cost subsidiary record totals $24,100 for H-101. The WIP control-account additions also total $24,100. That equality is the first reconciliation. It does not prove cutoff, existence, or entity accuracy, so the accountant also traces each line to its source and confirms it belongs to MBG rather than Riverton.

Now add an illustrative $1,900 excavator rental coded E001 and a $600 permit coded O001. The job total becomes $26,600, while the control-account rollup becomes: 1401 $3,200; 1402 $8,400; 1403 $1,900; 1404 $12,500; 1405 $600. Their sum is $26,600. If JCS shows $26,600 in job detail but only $24,700 in the mapped GL additions, the $1,900 variance points directly to the equipment line. A total-only comparison would show that something is wrong; category rollup shows where to investigate.

At period end, use a rollforward for each WIP control account: beginning WIP plus additions plus or minus reclasses minus transfers to cost of sales equals ending WIP. Keep job reclasses separate from external additions. Moving a cost from one job to another within the same WIP GL account changes subsidiary detail but has zero GL impact. Moving a cost between cost categories changes the WIP control accounts but not total WIP. When a completed home closes, the relevant accumulated cost transfers from WIP to cost of sales; it does not remain an asset indefinitely.

Predetermined overhead rate

Job-order systems often apply overhead using a predetermined rate: estimated production overhead divided by estimated allocation-base activity. If illustrative annual production overhead is $480,000 and expected direct-labor hours are 24,000, the rate is $20 per direct-labor hour. A job using 160 hours receives $3,200 of applied overhead. Actual overhead and applied overhead are compared at period end. Underapplied overhead means actual overhead exceeded applied overhead; overapplied means applied exceeded actual. The allocation base must have a causal or beneficial relationship to the cost pool.

Why the controls matter

A cost code should be granular enough to support estimating and accountability but stable enough to compare jobs. Creating a new code for every invoice makes trends meaningless. Using one broad code hides overruns. The chart of accounts should remain even more stable: it answers financial-reporting questions, while dimensions answer operational questions. This separation is a core design principle in accounting information systems.

Reconciliation must use exact account numbers and a consistent cutoff. The fictional case-source rule warns that JCS's “Acct Ending Bal” is not cumulative; calculate true ending balance from beginning balance plus year-to-date debits minus year-to-date credits. Also avoid substring searches: searching “1401” can capture unintended job-cost strings. Tie exact mapped detail to the exact GL account, then tie the combined 14xxxxx WIP balance to the trial balance. The MBG total of $14,480,000.00 is the anchor, not a substitute for job-level proof.

Measurement bases — actual, normal, and standard costing

The ICMA blueprint lists actual and normal costs and standard costs as distinct measurement concepts before it lists costing systems. They differ in only one place: how overhead enters the job.

BasisDirect materialsDirect laborOverhead
Actual costingActual quantity × actual priceActual hours × actual rateActual overhead × actual base
Normal costingActual quantity × actual priceActual hours × actual ratePredetermined rate × actual base
Standard costingStandard quantity × standard priceStandard hours × standard rateStandard rate × standard base allowed

Actual costing is the most faithful and the least timely: the actual overhead rate cannot be known until the period closes, and a monthly actual rate swings with seasonal volume. Normal costing solves the timing problem by fixing the rate in advance and accepting a year-end true-up. Standard costing goes further and prices the inputs too, which is what makes variance analysis possible. MBG job cost sheets in this course use normal costing unless a question says otherwise.

Worked example — a normal-costing job cost sheet, every step

All amounts here are illustrative. MBG budgets $480,000 of production overhead and 24,000 direct-labor hours for the year, so the predetermined overhead rate (POHR) is:

  • POHR = estimated overhead ÷ estimated allocation-base activity
  • POHR = $480,000 ÷ 24,000 direct-labor hours = $20.00 per direct-labor hour

Job H-104 accumulates the following during the year: framing and finish materials requisitioned $46,800 (cost code M001, GL 1402); 1,340 rough-carpenter hours at $32.00 per hour (cost code L004, GL 1401); and overhead applied on the same 1,340 hours (GL 1403 through 1405 pools).

Job cost sheet lineComputationAmount
Direct materialsRequisitions traced to H-104$46,800
Direct labor1,340 hours × $32.00$42,880
Applied overhead1,340 hours × $20.00 POHR$26,800
Total job cost$46,800 + $42,880 + $26,800$116,480

Read the third line carefully. The rate is estimated and the base is actual. Nothing on this sheet is the actual overhead MBG incurred. Applied overhead is a rate multiplied by a driver, and that is exactly the convention the app drill uses: applied overhead equals actual base multiplied by the predetermined rate.

Trap that loses the mark — applying the rate to the estimated base

The single most common error on a POHR question is multiplying the rate by the estimated 24,000 hours instead of the job or period's actual hours. That returns $480,000, which is the budget, not an application. Estimated hours appear only in the denominator when the rate is built. Once the rate exists, the estimate is never used again. Two numbers, two roles: the estimate builds the rate, the actual applies it.

Worked example — year-end over- and underapplied overhead and its disposition

Continue the illustrative year. MBG actually worked 23,650 direct-labor hours and actually incurred $497,300 of production overhead.

  • Overhead applied for the year = 23,650 hours × $20.00 = $473,000
  • Over- or (under)applied = applied − actual = $473,000 − $497,300 = ($24,300)

The sign convention matters and the app drill uses it: a positive result is overapplied, a negative result is underapplied. Here overhead is underapplied by $24,300, meaning jobs were charged $24,300 less overhead than the business actually consumed. Underapplied overhead therefore understates recorded cost and overstates reported gross profit until it is disposed of.

Two dispositions are acceptable. If the amount is immaterial, close the entire $24,300 to cost of sales, which increases cost of sales by $24,300. If it is material, prorate it across the accounts that still carry applied overhead. Suppose the pre-disposition balances are WIP $270,000, completed-but-unsold homes $180,000, and cost of sales $1,350,000.

AccountBalanceShare of $1,800,000Prorated underapplied
WIP (14xxxxx)$270,000$270,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 15.00%15.00% × $24,300 = $3,645
Completed homes$180,000$180,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 10.00%10.00% × $24,300 = $2,430
Cost of sales$1,350,000$1,350,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 75.00%75.00% × $24,300 = $18,225
Total$1,800,000100.00%$24,300

Prove the proration by footing the last column: $3,645 + $2,430 + $18,225 = $24,300. Every dollar of the underapplied balance lands somewhere; the disposition entry debits the three accounts and credits the overhead control account, leaving applied and actual overhead both at zero for the year.

Worked example — absorption versus variable costing

Whether fixed production overhead sits in WIP or in expense is a measurement-basis decision, not an arithmetic one. Under absorption (full) costing, fixed production overhead is a product cost that stays on the balance sheet inside unsold inventory. Under variable (direct) costing, fixed production overhead is a period cost expensed as incurred.

Take an illustrative prefabricated-panel line. MBG produced 30,000 panels, sold 26,000 panels, and incurred $600,000 of fixed production overhead.

  • Fixed overhead per unit = $600,000 ÷ 30,000 produced = $20.00 per panel
  • Units added to inventory = 30,000 produced − 26,000 sold = 4,000 panels
  • Fixed overhead deferred in inventory = $20.00 × 4,000 = $80,000

Absorption operating income therefore exceeds variable operating income by exactly $80,000. The general rule, and the convention the app drill uses, is: absorption income minus variable income equals fixed overhead per unit multiplied by (units produced − units sold). Build inventory and absorption reports higher income; draw inventory down and absorption reports lower income. If production equals sales, the two methods report identical income.

Trap that loses the mark — dividing fixed overhead by units sold

The per-unit fixed overhead rate is always built on units produced, because production is what the overhead supported. Dividing $600,000 by the 26,000 units sold gives $23.08 and a wrong $92,308 answer. Produced in the denominator, the produced-minus-sold gap in the multiplier.

Contrast — process costing and equivalent units

Job-order costing suits distinct, identifiable jobs. Process costing suits continuous, homogeneous output where no single unit is separately traced — a panel plant, a ready-mix operation, a millwork shop. Cost is accumulated by department and spread over equivalent units of production.

An equivalent unit converts partially finished work into a whole-unit equivalent. Materials are often added entirely at the start, while conversion (labor plus overhead) accrues evenly, so the two usually have different equivalent-unit totals.

Illustrative panel department, weighted-average method, for one month: 42,000 panels were completed and transferred out; ending WIP is 6,000 panels, 100% complete as to materials and 40% complete as to conversion.

  • Equivalent units — materials = 42,000 + (6,000 × 100%) = 48,000
  • Equivalent units — conversion = 42,000 + (6,000 × 40%) = 42,000 + 2,400 = 44,400

Weighted average blends beginning WIP cost with current cost, so the cost pools are: materials $91,000 in beginning WIP plus $293,000 added = $384,000; conversion $38,400 in beginning WIP plus $405,600 added = $444,000.

  • Cost per equivalent unit — materials = $384,000 ÷ 48,000 = $8.00
  • Cost per equivalent unit — conversion = $444,000 ÷ 44,400 = $10.00
  • Total cost per completed panel = $8.00 + $10.00 = $18.00

Now assign the cost. Transferred out = 42,000 × $18.00 = $756,000. Ending WIP = (6,000 × $8.00) + (2,400 × $10.00) = $48,000 + $24,000 = $72,000. Prove it: $756,000 + $72,000 = $828,000, and total cost to account for was $384,000 + $444,000 = $828,000. The two agree to the dollar, which is the process-costing equivalent of the job-to-GL tie described earlier in this lesson.

Trap that loses the mark — one completion percentage for both columns

Candidates lose the equivalent-units mark by applying the 40% conversion percentage to materials as well, producing 44,400 for both columns and a materials rate of $8.65 instead of $8.00. Materials added at the start of the process are 100% complete in ending WIP no matter how little conversion work has occurred. Always build two columns and state the percentage that belongs to each. The units completed and transferred out are 100% complete for every cost element, which is why they enter both columns at full count.

CPA Crossover — FAR

FAR asks whether costs qualify for capitalization and how assets and expenses are classified. The CMA emphasis is cost accumulation and managerial use; FAR adds recognition and presentation. For MBG, valid construction costs accumulate as a WIP/CIP asset while the related performance remains in process, subject to the applicable contract and inventory guidance. General inefficiency, abnormal waste, and unrelated administrative costs do not become assets merely because management assigns a job code. A dimension cannot override recognition rules.

Practice — perform the close test

  1. Select one entity and cutoff; never combine MBG and Riverton.
  2. Export exact-account GL activity for 1401–1405 and job-cost detail from JCS.
  3. Map every valid cost code to one WIP control account and quarantine invalid codes.
  4. Reconcile by job, control account, and total; explain every variance to $0.00.
  5. Trace samples to invoice, payroll, approval, and job evidence.
  6. Separate additions, job reclasses, category reclasses, and closeout transfers.
  7. Review stale WIP and completed jobs that should have transferred to cost of sales.

Recap: job-order costing answers “what did this job consume?” The GL answers “what financial resource or obligation changed?” Cost codes preserve detail; WIP control accounts preserve financial-statement integrity. A valid system posts both views, reconciles them exactly, and maintains entity and period boundaries.

flashcards.front: Are L004, M001, and S003 GL accounts?
flashcards.back: No. They are job cost codes/dimensions that map to WIP GL control accounts.

flashcards.front: Which WIP GL account receives material cost codes in the app mapping?
Job-cost subsidiary detail must reconcile to what?
flashcards.back: The exact mapped WIP GL control accounts for the same entity and cutoff.

flashcards.front: What is the basic WIP rollforward?
flashcards.back: Beginning WIP + additions ± reclasses − transfers to cost of sales = ending WIP.
A cost that can be economically traced to a specific job, contract, or cost object.

flashcards.front: How is a predetermined overhead rate calculated?
flashcards.back: Estimated production overhead divided by estimated allocation-base activity.

flashcards.front: What is the GL impact of moving cost between jobs within the same WIP account?
What is MBG's real WIP total used as the control anchor?

questions.q: An MBG invoice coded M001 for framing lumber should debit which mapped account?
questions.explain: M001 remains the job-cost dimension; material codes roll to the 1402 WIP control account.

questions.q: Illustrative estimated overhead is $360,000 and expected machine-hours are 18,000. What is the predetermined rate?
A cost moves from Job A to Job B but remains in 1402. What is the net GL effect?
questions.explain: The reclass changes job detail within the same control account, so equal debit and credit postings net to zero in the GL.

questions.q: Which cost is most likely a period cost rather than job WIP?
questions.explain: A general corporate activity does not create a traceable production benefit merely because someone assigns it a job code.

questions.q: Job detail totals $510,000 and mapped WIP GL additions total $507,500. What is the first defensible conclusion?
choices: There is a $2,500 reconciling difference to investigate
questions.explain: Neither ledger wins automatically. Identify and support the exact $2,500 difference before adjustment.

questions.q: Actual overhead is $105,000 and applied overhead is $98,000. Overhead is:
questions.explain: Actual exceeds applied by $7,000, so overhead is underapplied.

questions.q: Which control best prevents a cost code from corrupting the chart of accounts?
choices: Allow users to create GL accounts freely
Validate cost codes and map each to an approved WIP control account
Post all costs to one expense account
questions.explain: Validation preserves cost-code detail while limiting financial postings to approved control accounts.
